transcription.tex: This chapter develops addition and double-angle formulae, combines sine and cosine into one function, and uses these ideas to solve equations and model periodic motion.
\textbf{1. Addition formulae}\[\sin(a+b)=\sin a\cos b+\cos a\sin b\]
\textbf{3. Combining sine and cosine}\par Find the maximum of \(2\sin x+\cos x\) and where it occurs.
\textbf{4. Modelling}\par A tide can be modelled by \(x=R\sin(2\pi t/5+\alpha)\), where \(t\) is hours after midnight.

sourceMapping.method: Native text and LaTeX conversion; acceptance tracked separately

transcription.tex: Addition formulae handle sums and differences of angles.
\textbf{Do I need to memorise these?}\par They are in the formula booklet, but aim to memorise them, especially sine and cosine.

\textbf{How to remember}\par The first function on the right matches the left. Sine mixes sine and cosine; cosine keeps matching pairs. Sine keeps the sign, cosine changes it. Tangent keeps the sign on top and changes it underneath.\par The identities apply wherever both sides are defined.

transcription.tex: Why is \(\sin(A+B)\) not generally \(\sin A+\sin B\)? Give a counterexample.
Sine is a function, so it need not distribute over addition; similarly \((a+b)^2\) is not generally \(a^2+b^2\).

slides.title: Geometric Proof of the Sine Addition Formula

transcription.tex: Geometric proof (not required for the exam). Let \(OY=1\) make angle \(A+B\) with the horizontal, so \(XY=\sin(A+B)\).
1. Resolve the unit line along directions making angles \(A\) and \(A+\pi/2\) with the horizontal. The perpendicular components have lengths \(\cos B\) and \(\sin B\).
2. Their vertical components are \(\sin A\cos B\) and \(\cos A\sin B\).
3. Add the vertical lengths:\[\sin(A+B)=\sin A\cos B+\cos A\sin B.\]

transcription.tex: Use the sine addition formula to prove the formula for \(\sin(A-B)\).
\[\sin(A-B)=\sin(A+(-B))\]\[=\sin A\cos(-B)+\cos A\sin(-B)\]\[=\sin A\cos B-\cos A\sin B.\]
Prove the formula for \(\cos(A+B)\). Hint: use the complementary-angle relation.
\[\cos(A+B)=\sin((\pi/2-A)-B)\]\[=\sin(\pi/2-A)\cos B-\cos(\pi/2-A)\sin B\]\[=\cos A\cos B-\sin A\sin B.\]

transcription.tex: Edexcel C3 January 2012, Q8(a).\par Starting from the formulae for \(\sin(A+B)\) and \(\cos(A+B)\), prove that \(\tan(A+B)=\dfrac{\tan A+\tan B}{1-\tan A\tan B}\). (4 marks)

\[\tan(A+B)=\frac{\sin A\cos B+\cos A\sin B}{\cos A\cos B-\sin A\sin B}.\]\par Divide every numerator and denominator term by \(\cos A\cos B\):\[=\frac{\frac{\sin A\cos B}{\cos A\cos B}+\frac{\cos A\sin B}{\cos A\cos B}}{1-\frac{\sin A\sin B}{\cos A\cos B}}=\frac{\tan A+\tan B}{1-\tan A\tan B}.\]\par Work where both sides are defined.

transcription.tex: Given that \(2\sin (x+y)=3\cos \left(x-y\right)\) express \(\tan x\) in terms of \(\tan y\).

transcription.tex: \textbf{STEP I 2010 Q3}\par Show that\[\sin(x+y)-\sin(x-y)=2\cos x\sin y\]and deduce that\[\sin A-\sin B=2\cos\tfrac12(A+B)\sin\tfrac12(A-B).\]
\[\sin(x+y)-\sin(x-y)\]\[=\sin x\cos y+\cos x\sin y-(\sin x\cos y-\cos x\sin y)\]\[=2\cos x\sin y.\]\par Put \(x=(A+B)/2,y=(A-B)/2\) to obtain the required difference of sines.
\[\cos(x+y)-\cos(x-y)\]\[=\cos x\cos y-\sin x\sin y-(\cos x\cos y+\sin x\sin y)\]\[=-2\sin x\sin y.\]\par Use the same substitutions for \(x,y\).

The points \(P\), \(Q\), \(R\) and \(S\) have coordinates \((a\cos p,b\sin p)\), \((a\cos q,b\sin q)\), \((a\cos r,b\sin r)\) and \((a\cos s,b\sin s)\) respectively, where \(0\le p<q<r<s<2\pi\), and \(a\) and \(b\) are positive.\par Given that neither of the lines \(PQ\) and \(SR\) is vertical, show that these lines are parallel if and only if\[r+s-p-q=2\pi.\]

\[m_{PQ}=\frac{b(\sin q-\sin p)}{a(\cos q-\cos p)}\]\[=\frac{2b\cos((p+q)/2)\sin((q-p)/2)}{-2a\sin((p+q)/2)\sin((q-p)/2)}\]\[=-\frac ba\cot\frac{p+q}{2}.\]\par Similarly \(m_{SR}=-(b/a)\cot((r+s)/2)\). Equal slopes occur iff \((r+s-p-q)/2=k\pi\). Since \(0<r+s-p-q<4\pi\), only \(k=1\) is possible: the difference is \(2\pi\). Conversely this difference gives equal slopes.

transcription.tex: Write \(R\cos(2\theta+\alpha)=R\cos2\theta\cos\alpha-R\sin2\theta\sin\alpha\).\par Comparing coefficients: \(R\cos\alpha=1\), \(R\sin\alpha=\sqrt3\).\par Divide: \(\tan\alpha=\sqrt3\), hence \(\alpha=\pi/3\). Square and add: \(R^2=1+3=4\), so \(R=2\).\[\cos2\theta-\sqrt3\sin2\theta=2\cos(2\theta+\pi/3).\]

transcription.tex: STEP I 2005 Q4.\par (a) Given that \(\cos\theta=\tfrac35\) and that \(\tfrac{3\pi}2\le\theta\le2\pi\), show that \(\sin2\theta=-\tfrac{24}{25}\), and evaluate \(\cos3\theta\).\par (b) Prove the identity \(\tan3\theta=\dfrac{3\tan\theta-\tan^3\theta}{1-3\tan^2\theta}\). Hence evaluate \(\tan\theta\), given that \(\tan3\theta=\tfrac{11}2\) and that \(\tfrac\pi4\le\theta\le\tfrac\pi2\).

(b) Put \(t=\tan\theta\). Using \(\tan(2\theta+\theta)\):\[\tan3\theta=\frac{2t/(1-t^2)+t}{1-2t^2/(1-t^2)}=\frac{3t-t^3}{1-3t^2}.\]\par The triple-angle identity extends wherever both final sides are defined.\[2t^3-33t^2-6t+11=0\]\[(2t-1)(t^2-16t-11)=0.\]\par Roots: \(1/2,8\pm\sqrt{75}\). The interval requires \(t\ge1\) and excludes \(\theta=\pi/2\) from the given equation, so \(t=8+\sqrt{75}\).

transcription.tex: Edexcel C3 June 2015 Q8.\par a. Prove that \(\sec2A+\tan2A=\frac{\cos A+\sin A}{\cos A-\sin A}\), \(A\ne(2n+1)\pi/4\), \(n\in\mathbb Z\). (5 marks)
Tip: the denominator needs a \(\cos A-\sin A\) factor, so use \(\cos2A=\cos^2A-\sin^2A\).

Another strategy is to work backwards from the desired result, multiplying by \((\cos A+\sin A)/(\cos A+\sin A)\). This suggests the squared numerator. Present reversible steps and check the factors are nonzero.

\[\sec2A+\tan2A=\frac{1+\sin2A}{\cos2A}\]\[=\frac{\cos^2A+2\sin A\cos A+\sin^2A}{(\cos A-\sin A)(\cos A+\sin A)}\]\[=\frac{(\cos A+\sin A)^2}{(\cos A-\sin A)(\cos A+\sin A)}=\frac{\cos A+\sin A}{\cos A-\sin A}.\]
(b) Hence solve, for \(0\le\theta<2\pi\), \(\sec2\theta+\tan2\theta=\tfrac12\). Give your answers to 3 decimal places. (4 marks)

transcription.tex: June 2013 (Withdrawn) Q8.\par (a) Express \(9\cos\theta-2\sin\theta\) in the form \(R\cos(\theta+\alpha)\), where \(R>0\) and \(0<\alpha<\tfrac\pi2\). Give the exact value of \(R\) and give the value of \(\alpha\) to 4 decimal places. (3 marks)\par (b)(i) State the maximum value of \(9\cos\theta-2\sin\theta\).\par (ii) Find the value of \(\theta\), for \(0<\theta<2\pi\), at which this maximum occurs. (3 marks)
Maximum \(\sqrt{85}\), since cosine is at most 1.

Ruth models the height \(H\) above the ground of a passenger on a Ferris wheel by the equation \(H=10-9\cos(\tfrac{\pi t}5)+2\sin(\tfrac{\pi t}5)\), where \(H\) is measured in metres and \(t\) is the time in minutes after the wheel starts turning.\par (c) Calculate the maximum value of \(H\) predicted by this model, and the value of \(t\), when this maximum first occurs. Give your answers to 2 decimal places. (4 marks)\par (d) Determine the time for the Ferris wheel to complete two revolutions. (2 marks)
One revolution takes \(2\pi/(\pi/5)=10\) minutes, so two take \(20\) minutes.
Sine and cosine model oscillations such as tides, pendulums and sound waves.

transcription.tex: June 2010 Q7.\par (a) Express \(2\sin\theta-1.5\cos\theta\) in the form \(R\sin(\theta-\alpha)\), where \(R>0\) and \(0<\alpha<\tfrac\pi2\). Give the value of \(\alpha\) to 4 decimal places. (3 marks)\par (b)(i) Find the maximum value of \(2\sin\theta-1.5\cos\theta\).\par (ii) Find the value of \(\theta\), for \(0\le\theta<\pi\), at which this maximum occurs. (3 marks)
Maximum \(2.5\), since sine is at most 1.

Tom models the height of sea water, \(H\) metres, on a particular day by the equation \(H=6+2\sin(\tfrac{4\pi t}{25})-1.5\cos(\tfrac{4\pi t}{25}),\ 0\le t<12\), where \(t\) hours is the number of hours after midday.\par (c) Calculate the maximum value of \(H\) predicted by this model and the value of \(t\), to 2 decimal places, when this maximum occurs. (3 marks)\par (d) Calculate, to the nearest minute, the times when the height of sea water is predicted, by this model, to be 7 metres. (6 marks)
\[H=6+2.5\sin(4\pi t/25-\alpha).\]\par Maximum \(8.5\) m, at \(t=25(\pi/2+\alpha)/(4\pi)=4.41\) hours after midday.

\[\sin(4\pi t/25-\alpha)=0.4.\]\par Let \(\beta=\arcsin0.4\). Within the time interval:\[t=\frac{25}{4\pi}(\alpha+\beta),\quad\frac{25}{4\pi}(\alpha+\pi-\beta).\]\par Thus the times are 14:06 and 18:43.
Tip: substitute \(\theta=4\pi t/25\) when using part (a).

transcription.tex: (a) Express \(65\cos\theta-20\sin\theta\) in the form \(R\cos(\theta+\alpha)\), where \(R>0\) and \(0<\alpha<\tfrac\pi2\). Give the value of \(\alpha\) correct to 4 decimal places.\par A city wants to build a large circular wheel as a tourist attraction.\par The height of a tourist on the circular wheel is modelled by the equation\par \(H=70-65\cos0.2t+20\sin0.2t\) where \(H\) is the height of the tourist above the ground in metres, \(t\) is the number of minutes after boarding\par and the angles are given in radians. Find:\par (b) the maximum height of the wheel\par (c) the time for one complete revolution\par (d) the number of minutes the tourist will be over 100 m above the ground in each revolution.

(d) \[H>100\iff\cos(0.2t+\alpha)<-30/R.\]\par Let \(\beta=\arccos(-30/R)\). The interval above 100 m in one cycle has angular length \(2\pi-2\beta\).\[\text{Duration}=\frac{2\pi-2\beta}{0.2}=11.1\text{ minutes (1 d.p.)}.\]\par The first crossing times are about 8.646 and 19.785 minutes.
